item.title: GraphGen Initial Release Adds Knowledge-Guided Synthetic Data for LLMs
item.description:
GraphGen Initial Release Adds Knowledge-Guided Synthetic Data for LLMs

The initial version of GraphGen has been released, a framework designed for synthetic data generation guided by knowledge graphs. It constructs fine-grained knowledge graphs from source text and identifies knowledge gaps in Large Language Models (LLMs) using the expected calibration error metric, prioritizing QA pairs that target high-value, long-tail knowledge. The associated paper, “Knowledge-to-Verification: Exploring RLVR for LLMs in Knowledge-Intensive Domains,” has been accepted to the ACL 2026 Main Conference.

🧩 How it works

GraphGen operates by first constructing a fine-grained knowledge graph from the source text. It then identifies knowledge gaps in LLMs using the expected calibration error metric, which allows it to prioritize the generation of QA pairs that target high-value, long-tail knowledge. The framework incorporates multi-hop neighborhood sampling to capture complex relational information and employs style-controlled generation to diversify the resulting QA data. Additionally, support for community detection in knowledge graphs using the Leiden algorithm enables the synthesis of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data.

⚙️ Key details

GraphGen supports a range of input sources and data formats, including HuggingFace Datasets and PDF files processed via MinerU. It also supports Visual Question Answering (VQA) data generation. The framework includes knowledge graph evaluation metrics covering:

  • Accuracy (entity/relation)
  • Consistency (conflict detection)
  • Structural robustness (noise, connectivity, degree distribution)

The backend infrastructure includes support for rocksdb as a key-value storage backend and kuzudb as a graph database backend. Local inference is supported via vllm. For distributed execution and resource management, the data generation pipeline has been refactored using Ray.

🔌 Integration and Clients

After data generation, users can fine-tune their LLMs using LLaMA-Factory and xtuner. GraphGen supports several new LLM clients and inference backends:

Component Function/Details
Ollama_client Supported LLM client
http_client Supported LLM client
HuggingFace Transformers Supported inference backend
SGLang Supported inference backend
vllm Local inference backend

Search support has been added for several back-ends and databases, enabling the extraction of specific data types:

  • Google, Bing, and Wikipedia search back-ends.
  • UniProt, NCBI, and RNAcentral databases for extracting DNA and RNA data from bioinformatics sources.

📈 Data Modalities

LLM benchmark synthesis within GraphGen supports multiple question formats, which is ideal for education:

  • Single-choice
  • Multiple-choice
  • Fill-in-the-blank
  • True-or-false

🚀 Availability

The initial version of GraphGen is available with auto-updating Gradio demos hosted on Hugging Face and ModelScope.

#GraphGen #KnowledgeGraphs #SyntheticData #LLMTraining #ACL2026

Source: InternScience/GraphGen

item.title: Nucleoid adds terminal workspace, bare-word syntax, and comment updates
item.description:
Nucleoid adds terminal workspace, bare-word syntax, and comment updates

Nucleoid has updated its developer experience and language syntax with a new full-screen terminal workspace, support for bare-word assignments, and changes to how comments and conditional logic are handled.

🔍 Overview

Nucleoid is a next-generation logic programming language built on structured objects and their relationships, extending the traditional Knowledge Graph. It uses a minimum-token syntax for logic representation and a declarative execution model, eliminating the need for LLMs to manually manage control flow, state propagation, and other imperative constructs.

🧩 How it works

The new interactive interface offers a top-level tab layout, with two tabs reserved for future views. A multiline editor sits at the bottom, featuring autocomplete for keywords, built-ins, and model properties, plus in-session input and result history. Results can be inspected in Text, JSON, or Table formats without re-running the program; arrays of objects render as table rows, while other JSON values display in property/value or index/value views.

Key input behaviors include:

  • Enter inserts a newline.
  • F5 runs the entire editor content.
  • Ctrl-J inserts an automatically indented newline.
  • Tab accepts autocomplete or indents.
  • Ctrl-Space opens suggestions.
  • Ctrl-P / Ctrl-N recalls input while preserving an unfinished draft.
  • F1-F3 switch tabs, F6 changes the result view, and Ctrl-Up / Ctrl-Down select earlier results.
  • Mouse clicks select tabs, views, and results; click/drag edits the cursor/selection, and the wheel scrolls individual panes.
  • Ctrl-C cancels input, Ctrl-Q exits, and .help lists all controls.

⚙️ Key details

  • Assignment Syntax: Assignments can be written as target is value. Quotes are optional around a single word. For example, a is 5 and o.x is "good" are valid. If the value is a bare word that does not match a defined variable, class, function, or built-in, it stores its own text.
  • Conditional Branches: In conditionals like a is A if c else B, a bare word in a branch is read as a variable, class, function, or built-in if it exists; otherwise, it reads as its own text. Parenthesized operands are not treated as words, so a is (A if c else B) requires A and B to be defined.
  • List and Dictionary Items: Inside is values, list items, dictionary values, or named arguments can also be bare words.
  • Comments: Hash (#), double-slash (//), and non-nesting block comments (/* ... */) all work in files and interactive interfaces. Comments take delimiter priority outside literals, meaning // is a comment, not an empty regex (use /(?:)/ for an empty-matching regex). Comments retain newlines and source positions and cannot join tokens or supply indentation. Unclosed block comments report SyntaxError: Unterminated block comment at its opening slash.
  • Plain Mode: Running nucleoid --plain provides a line-oriented interface. Piped stdin or redirected stdout automatically selects this mode. Body lines are prefilled with indentation after the .. prompt, and blank lines submit the block.

🚀 Availability

Install the CLI from crates.io using the command: cargo install nucleoid. The standard nucleoid command opens the full-screen terminal workspace from any directory. File execution and the --json and --graph flags retain their existing behavior. References NUC 76, NUC 93, and NUC 94 document the removal of the --c-style-comments, --is-assignment, and --conditional-words flags, respectively.

#Nucleoid #LogicProgramming #CLI #KnowledgeGraph #Rust

Source: NucleoidAI/Nucleoid

item.title: Study Finds Limited Gains from Better Confidence in LLM‑Built Knowledge‑Graph Audits
item.description:
Study Finds Limited Gains from Better Confidence in LLM‑Built Knowledge‑Graph Audits

Confidence estimates are used to steer human review of knowledge graphs constructed by large language models (LLMs), but this new work shows that higher‑quality confidence predictions do not automatically translate into substantially better audit outcomes.

🔍 Overview

  • Paper title: When Does Better Confidence Improve a Knowledge‑Graph Audit?
  • Submitted on 4 Nov 2026 to Computer Science > Computation and Language.
  • Focus: quantifying the practical value of improved confidence estimates when auditing LLM‑generated knowledge graphs.

🧩 How the Study Is Structured

  • Investigates three dimensions of the gap between confidence and audit performance: repairability, selection headroom, and label validity.
  • Models non‑adaptive auditing as a budgeted covering problem.
  • Derives the minimal decision‑relevant error statistics and bounds the regret of scalar‑preserving first‑order planning by a structural mass \(Δ^{\mathrm{cl}}\).

⚙️ Experimental Setup

  • Simulated ideal repair against benchmark‑aligned labels.
  • Tested five extraction configurations across two cross‑document graphs taken from the Re‑DocRED dataset.
  • After repair, performed frozen confirmation on a held‑out test set and replicated the process on 500 hash‑selected training documents.

📊 Key Findings

  • On held‑out cross‑document graphs, an error‑rate × fan‑out queue leaves 3.98–4.74 percentage points more errors than a joint model using the same actions.
  • Allowing shared actions for the joint planner cuts residual errors by 0.89–1.43 points compared with fact‑only plans (point‑estimate view).
  • Equivalence between joint and independent‑block models remains inconclusive.
  • Generic LLM verification improves three of four model‑budget configurations on each held‑out set.
  • LLM adjudication uncovers possible benchmark omissions.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Better confidence does not guarantee large audit improvements; real gains are modest and contingent on planner design.
  • Joint planning with shared actions can yield small but measurable error reductions.
  • Findings highlight the need for more nuanced audit strategies beyond simply tightening confidence estimates.

(All data and code associated with the study are available through the ancillary files linked in the submission.)

#knowledgegraphs #LLM #audit #confidence #NLP

Source: When Does Better Confidence Improve a Knowledge-Graph Audit?

item.title: 🧠 DRG: The Missing Link Between LLMs and Deterministic Reasoning
item.description:
🧠 DRG: The Missing Link Between LLMs and Deterministic Reasoning

Summary: Discover how Deterministic Reasoning Graphs (DRGs) are transforming AI by bringing structure and precision to Large Language Models. This post explores DRG’s core principles, key applications like Chain of Reasoning Graphs (CoRG), and how they enable truly deterministic agent reasoning—all while avoiding the probabilistic pitfalls of traditional LLM approaches.

🔍 Introducing Deterministic Reasoning: Beyond Probabilistic AI

The rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) has transformed how we interact with artificial intelligence. Yet despite their impressive capabilities, these models remain fundamentally probabilistic—making them inherently unpredictable when absolute reliability is required. Enter the Deterministic Reasoning Graph (DRG), a paradigm shift in how we organize and process information that promises to eliminate this indeterminism.

Unlike traditional approaches, DRGs aren’t about building new LLM architectures or learning algorithms. Instead, they offer a structured methodology for capturing and enforcing reasoning and decision-making patterns within specific domains. This structure serves as a foundation for more controlled, predictable AI applications—from advanced retrieval to intelligent agents.

📸 See illustration below showing the conceptual difference between probabilistic LLM responses and a DRG-guided deterministic pathway

🏗️ The Architecture: What Makes DRGs Different

At its core, a DRG structures information by explicitly encoding reasoning processes in graph form. This isn’t just another knowledge graph—it’s a formalized representation of 𝗵𝗼𝘄 reasoning should occur within a defined context.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀:

  1. CoRG (Chain of Reasoning Graph) 🔄 — A domain-specific RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) that structures information retrieval based on explicit reasoning steps.

  2. Discriminator ✅ — A verification mechanism that validates LLM outputs against logical expectations.

  3. Dataset Generator 📊 — A system for creating training data with built-in reasoning consistency.

  4. Conversational and Decision-Making Agents 🤖 — AI agents whose actions are guided by explicit, deterministic reasoning trees.

For those familiar with the Chain of Tasks concept (see Episode 13 referenced in the original text), CoRG builds upon this idea by formalizing inference sequences. The first step is typically context classification by an LLM, followed by a graph database query using that classification. The retrieved context then informs dynamic prompt tuning before the final inference step.

📸 See diagram illustrating the CoRG workflow from initial query through context classification to final response generation

🤖 Agents Reimagined: From Probabilistic to Deterministic

What truly sets DRG apart is its application to agentic architectures. While systems like LangGraph offer conditional routing, they typically operate at a coarser granularity than DRG-based approaches.

𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗚𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗵:

Aspect LangGraph DRG
Routing Type Explicit conditional (if, match, switch) Semantic and contextual
Logic Decision tree with condition-based routing Decision tree applied to a graph (no algorithmic limitations)

DRG takes agent reasoning to a new level by encoding not just simple conditionals but rich semantic relationships. These include concepts like “triggered after,” “inherits from,” “modulated by,” and “validates”—transforming system architecture into a controllable, unambiguous logical framework.

🔥 The result? Agents that reason with domain-specific precision rather than general probabilistic tendencies.

🌐 Implementing DRG: Domain Expertise Meets AI

The 𝙘𝙤𝙧𝙚 𝙥𝙧𝙞𝙣𝙘𝙞𝙥𝙡𝙚 behind successful DRG implementation lies in its collaborative design process. The graph structure isn’t created in isolation by AI engineers—it’s crafted alongside business teams or scientific domain experts according to use-case-specific ontologies.

This domain-grounded approach ensures that the resulting constraints applied to the LLM reflect actual business logic or scientific reasoning patterns. By anchoring AI reasoning in expert-defined structures, DRG bridges the gap between human expertise and machine intelligence.

To guarantee deterministic results, fine-tuning the LLM becomes essential. The graph queries incorporate not just simple lookups but complex patterns involving nodes, relationships, and clusters—though the original text notes this complexity is somewhat simplified for clarity.

📸 See example of a domain-specific DRG showing reasoning pathways for a financial decision-making agent

🚀 Why DRG Matters: The Future of Controllable AI

The implications of DRG extend far beyond technical novelty. In a world increasingly concerned about AI unpredictability and hallucinations, DRG offers a path toward systems that reason in ways that are:

  • 🔍 Inspectable — reasoning steps are explicit and can be reviewed
  • 🔄 Reproducible — given the same inputs, the system follows the same reasoning path
  • 🛠️ Fixable — when errors occur, specific reasoning steps can be corrected
  • 📊 Auditable — the entire decision process can be documented and evaluated

For organizations deploying AI in high-stakes environments—healthcare, finance, legal, or critical infrastructure—this shift from probabilistic to deterministic reasoning could be transformative.

💭 Conclusion: The Deterministic Path Forward

As LLMs continue to evolve, the integration of deterministic reasoning structures like DRG represents a crucial step toward more reliable, trustworthy AI systems. By explicitly encoding reasoning pathways rather than hoping they emerge from statistical patterns, we gain greater control over how AI systems make decisions.

The question now isn’t whether deterministic approaches like DRG will complement probabilistic models, but how quickly they’ll become essential components in mission-critical AI applications. As domains requiring absolute precision continue adopting AI, the value of structured reasoning will only increase.

What would your organization’s reasoning graph look like? How might explicitly structuring domain knowledge transform your AI applications from probabilistic guesswork to deterministic precision?
